questions.q: What is the integer factoring problem?
options: Given a composite integer N, find integers p and q greater than 1 such that N = p × q
Given a prime number, prove that it is prime
Given two primes, compute their product as quickly as possible
Given a public key, generate a matching private key from scratch with no other input
questions.explain: Factoring asks for the reverse direction of multiplication: starting from the product N, recover the factors p and q.

questions.q: Why does RSA's security depend on the integer factoring problem specifically?
options: RSA's public modulus N is the product of two secret primes p and q; recovering p and q from N would let an attacker reconstruct the private key
RSA uses factoring only to generate random numbers during key creation, with no further relevance
Factoring is unrelated to RSA; RSA's security comes entirely from the length of the password used
RSA requires factoring to encrypt each message, so faster factoring would only speed up legitimate encryption, not attacks
questions.explain: RSA's public key exposes N = p·q. The private key depends on p and q individually, so an attacker who can factor N can break the scheme.

questions.q: What is the complexity of the best known classical factoring algorithm (the General Number Field Sieve), honestly stated?
options: Sub-exponential time -- slower-growing than brute-force exponential search, but still faster-growing than any polynomial in the bit-length
Polynomial time, the same order of growth as Shor's quantum algorithm
Constant time, independent of the size of N
Logarithmic time, making factoring trivially fast for any N
questions.explain: GNFS runs in roughly exp(O(n^(1/3)(log n)^(2/3))) time for an n-bit N -- genuinely sub-exponential, but not polynomial, which is why larger RSA key sizes remain classically hard.

questions.q: Why is Shor's algorithm's speedup described as categorically different from Grover's algorithm's speedup?
options: Grover's algorithm gives a bounded quadratic speedup within the same complexity class, while Shor's algorithm moves factoring from sub-exponential (classical) into polynomial time (quantum) -- a change of complexity class, not just a constant improvement
Grover's algorithm and Shor's algorithm both give exactly the same speedup, so there is no real difference
Shor's algorithm only works on even numbers, while Grover's algorithm works on any input
Grover's algorithm is slower than classical search, while Shor's algorithm is slower than classical factoring
questions.explain: Grover's speedup is quadratic (O(sqrt(N)) vs O(N)), still exponential-to-exponential or polynomial-to-polynomial. Shor's result reclassifies factoring itself from sub-exponential to polynomial.

questions.q: Why do cryptographers consider the factoring problem's classical difficulty a computational claim rather than a mathematical impossibility?
options: No one has proven that fast classical factoring is impossible -- only that no fast classical algorithm has been found so far, which is a claim about the current state of knowledge, not a proof of inherent hardness
It has been mathematically proven that factoring is impossible for any computer, quantum or classical
Factoring is provably impossible in principle, the same way dividing by zero is undefined
The claim is purely a legal one set by cryptography standards bodies, with no mathematical content
questions.explain: RSA's security rests on the absence of a known fast classical algorithm, not on a proof that none can exist -- which is exactly why a fast algorithm (Shor's, on a quantum computer) changes the picture.
